The docket office has 10 business days to respond to such requests. With the exception of such material, publicly available docket materials are available electronically at 
                        https://www.regulations.gov
                         or on EPA computers in the docket office reading room at the EPA Docket Center, WJC West Building, Room Number 3334, 1301 Constitution Ave. NW, Washington, DC. The Public Reading Room hours of operation are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. ET, Monday through Friday (except for Federal holidays). The telephone number for the Public Reading Room is (202) 566-1744, and the telephone number for the EPA Docket Center is (202) 566-1742.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    The EPA finalized the Lime Manufacturing NESHAP technology review on July 16, 2024.[] 
                    
                     Following publication of this final rule, the EPA discovered an error in the regulatory text and is correcting the error in this action.
                
                    Specifically, the EPA is revising the Lime Manufacturing NESHAP July 16, 2024, final rule (2024 final rule) to correct 40 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) part 63 section 7114. In the 2024 final rule amendatory text, 40 CFR 63.7114 was revised to include two new paragraphs describing the requirements for the emissions averaging compliance option. These additions were added to the section as paragraphs (b) and (c). Paragraph (c)(2) instructs lime manufacturing plants that chose to comply with emissions averaging for HCl or mercury to develop and submit to the applicable regulatory authority for review and approval, an implementation plan for emission averaging no later than 180 days before the date the facility intends to demonstrate compliance. The EPA is revising the 180-day plan submittal requirement to 60 days, as the Agency intended. In the 2024 final rule preamble, under section 
                    E. What other changes have been made to the NESHAP?,
                     the EPA explains that the deadline for submitting the emissions averaging plan before the compliance demonstration was adjusted from 180 days, as proposed, to 60 days. Following publication of the 2024 final rule, the EPA discovered the regulatory text was not updated to reflect this change.
                
The correction in this action makes the regulatory text consistent with what the preamble to the 2024 final rule describes. The EPA's authority for the rulemaking procedures followed in this action is provided by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. 553. In general, an agency issuing a rule must provide prior notice and an opportunity for public comment, but APA section 553(b)(B) includes an exemption from notice-and-comment requirements “when the agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefor in the rule issued) that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” The EPA has determined that there is good cause for making this rule final without prior proposal and opportunity for comment because the changes to the rule are minor, noncontroversial in nature, and correct an inadvertent typographical error. The change aligns regulatory text with the EPA's expressed intent in the 2024 final rule preamble and does not substantively change the requirements of the 2024 final rule except to the extent necessary to align the regulatory text with the EPA's intent, which the preamble expressly states. Thus, the corrected regulatory text in this action has already had notice and opportunity for public comment, rendering further notice and opportunity for public comment unnecessary. The EPA finds that this constitutes good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B).

AGENCY:
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule revises the Conditions for Coverage for Organ Procurement Organizations (OPOs) to clarify outstanding procedural questions and provide additional operational flexibility for OPOs to achieve high performance resulting in the successful procurement, distribution, and transplantation of more life-saving organs. This rule revises definitions, revises the designation requirements for OPOs, clarifies when an OPO's service area is open for competition, and updates the process for appeals. We are committed to holding all OPOs accountable for their performance and this final rule does not revise the focus on improving the volume of donors and transplants assessed in the outcome measures or the tier structure used for re-certification and de-certification of OPOs.
DATES:
These regulations are effective on January 4, 2027.
At any given time, at least 100,000 people are on the waiting list for a lifesaving transplant and every 8 minutes, another person is added to the transplant waiting list.[1]
Many individuals on the organ transplant waiting list will wait several years for a suitable donor, while others will die before an organ becomes available. A variety of factors affect wait times for an organ transplant, including how well a waitlisted individual matches with available donors, how sick the person is, and the availability of organs in the region. Despite continued growth in organ donation, procurement, and transplantation, the need for transplantable organs continues to grow. The success of organ procurement organizations (OPOs) in performing their essential functions (obtaining consent for donation, working with the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) to match organs with recipients, procuring viable organs, and delivering those organs in transplantable condition to their recipients) is a rate limiting factor on the success of the entire organ transplant system. Therefore, optimal performance of OPOs is critical to ensure that the maximum possible number of transplantable human organs are available to the yearly average of more than 100,000 seriously ill people on waiting lists for a lifesaving organ transplant.
In 2019, President Trump issued Executive Order 13879 “Advancing American Kidney Health,” directing the Secretary to enhance the procurement and utilization of organs available through deceased donation and to establish more transparent, reliable, and enforceable metrics for evaluating an OPO's performance. In response, CMS published the final rule, “Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Organ Procurement Organization Conditions for Coverage: Revisions to the Outcome Measure Requirements for Organ Procurement Organizations” in 2020 (85 FR 77898, referred to hereafter as the December 2020 OPO final rule), which, among other changes, revised the previous outcome measures to drive performance improvement and increase the number of transplantable organs. OPOs are evaluated on their performance on both the donor and transplantation measures. Since publishing the December 2020 OPO final rule, CMS has received many inquiries from OPOs and others seeking clarification on operational and administrative elements. These inquiries increased in frequency and volume as the system moved closer to the end of the 2022-2026 re-certification cycle. Therefore, CMS published a proposed rule, “Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Organ Procurement Organization Conditions for Coverage: Revisions to the Outcome Measure Requirements for Organ Procurement Organizations” on January 30, 2026 (91 FR 4190, hereinafter referred to as the January 2026 OPO proposed rule).
The proposed rule contained operational and administrative provisions which would govern the competition process, provide programmatic clarity, and address interested party requests for additional guidance. Additionally, the proposed rule contained provisions aimed at driving further quality and improvement in OPO operations, reflecting our continued commitment to enhancing the organ procurement and transplant system, and better serving prospective organ donors, their families, and patients on the transplant waitlist.
B. Severability
To the extent a court may enjoin any part of the rule, the Department intends that other provisions or parts of provisions should remain in effect. Any provision of this rule held to be invalid or unenforceable by its terms, or as applied to any person or circumstance, shall be construed so as to continue to give maximum effect to the provisions as permitted by law, unless such holding shall be one of utter invalidity or unenforceability, in which event the provision shall be severable from this rule and shall not affect the remainder thereof or the application of the provision to persons not similarly situated or to dissimilar circumstances.
C. Summary of Costs and Benefits
This final rule is important due to its functional relationship to the December 2020 OPO final rule. Its purpose is to clarify and refine operational and administrative requirements related to OPO designation, re-certification, competition, appeals, information management, and Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI), while maintaining the accountability framework established in the December 2020 OPO final rule.
We estimate that this final rule will cost approximately $16.5 million in the first year and $7.9 million annually thereafter. These costs are incremental to the broader framework established in the December 2020 OPO final rule and reflect targeted operational and administrative refinements rather than fundamental system restructuring. We also estimate that this final rule will result in approximately $598,000 in annual benefits due to reduced implementation inquiry and compliance-interpretation burden, as well as an additional one-time benefit associated with clarified requirements and implementation efficiencies.

articles.full_text: The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS or Department) issues this rule to revise the regulation implementing section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (section 504) as it applies to recipients of HHS funding (entitled "Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability in Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance," ("2024 Final Rule")), published on May 9, 2024. This rule clarifies that the Department interprets the statutory exclusion of "gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments" from the terms "individual with a disability" and "disability" set forth in our regulations to encompass "gender dysphoria not resulting from a physical impairment" for purposes of the regulation. This clarification is necessary to resolve ambiguity introduced in the preamble to the 2024 Final Rule and to ensure compliance with the best reading of the governing statute.
